newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper threatens to ban looming strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper threatens to ban looming strike.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper threatened Friday to ban a national strike due to begin next week, warning the movement could be infiltrated by leftist guerrillas.

He warned that the planned industrial action by some 800,000 public sector workers, scheduled to begin February 11, was being driven by politics rather than labor issues and pledged to ensure that all vital services were maintained.

"Groups are looking to take advantage of the strike, including the clear participation of subversive groups...The interruption of any essential public services will immediately be declared illegal," Samper said in a speech at the national palace.

State workers are protesting below-inflation wage rises, growing restrictions on labor rights, and what they fear are government plans for the creeping privatization of key industries including telephones and oil.

Negotiations between the government and labor leaders broke down Thursday after the chief prosecutor's office announced legal action against workers from the state phone company Telecom and a judge jailed an oil workers' leader for seven years on charges of rebellion.
If the indefinite strike goes ahead, it could paralyze key sectors including oil, telecommunications, health and transport.
Labor analysts say it could be bigger than Colombia's last major strike in 1977, when 20 workers were killed in a day of street protests in Bogota.

Wilson Borja, head of the main state workers' union FENALTRASE, rejected Samper's claims. He said the labor movement was not linked to guerrillas and that the aim of the strike was to press for better conditions, not to topple the government.
But some of those groups backing the strike, including the oil workers' union USO and the Telecom workers are known for their radical, left-wing political stances.

At least 10 USO members are currently in custody, charged with dynamiting some of the country's key oil installations and belonging to the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest guerrilla force.

It was still unclear early Friday afternoon if the government would be able to kickstart talks aimed at averting the strike. Union representatives met with Chief Prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso and Interior Minister Horacio Serpa Friday morning.

"I think the conditions may be there to resume negotiations this afternoon," said Luis Eduardo Garzon, head of the Communist-controlled Unitary Workers' Confederation (CUT), which represents both public and private sector employees.
